FAILURES AND ARRANGEMENTS.
[It must not be overlooked that in many cases creditors whose names are published in these lists hold security for their debts, sometimes for the full amount.]

ELLIOTT, SAMUEL.—An adjourned sitting for public examination under the failure of Samuel Elliott, described as a joinery and moulding manufacturer, of Newbury and Old Broad Street, E.C., was held on Thursday. The accounts showed liabilities expected to rank, with assets £8,552.
Mr. H. Brougham attended as Official Receiver; Mr. Street (Ward, Perks, & M'Kay) appeared for the trustee; and Mr. Lucas for the debtor.
The debtor was examined by Mr. Street, and stated that he first found himself in difficulties in 1888, after he began to develop his smoke patents. In that year he approached his bankers with a view to obtaining assistance, and they were now creditors for over £50,000. It was true that since 1888 in nearly every case in which his creditors were given bills for goods he was either sued for the amount due or obtained the renewal of the bills. During the last six years about 800 writs had been issued against him.
Mr. Street: How do you justify your trading since 1888 and incurring liabilities to the extent of £100,000?
The debtor said he was always led to believe that his smoke patents were of considerable value. He could not say whether his creditors were told that the bills given them were accommodation bills.
Mr. Street: Is it not a fact that you got a clerk to sign accommodation bills, paying him 5s. on each occasion for his signature?
The debtor admitted this to be so. He said these bills were handed to creditors in respect of goods, but he made no representation as to their being trade bills.
Mr. Street: Are there not some hundreds of these bills?
The debtor said there were. Since March, 1894, he had expended in law costs in respect of executions about £3,500.
Mr. Street: During all this time you were obtaining goods from merchants. Did you not think it would be right to call your creditors together?
The debtor said he did not think it was necessary to do so, as he was expecting to realise his smoke patents.
The examination was ordered to be concluded.

MANSBRIDGE, JOSIAH, builder, 19, Finsbury Circus, E.C.—The bankrupt attended for his public examination on Tuesday, before Mr. Registrar Brougham, his accounts showing unsecured debts £258 5s. 9d.; debts fully secured £22,232 19s. 10d.; and debts partly secured £2,876 13s. 5d., the securities being valued at £2,097 0s. 2d.; assets £1,037 1s. 2d. In reply to Mr. E. L. Hough,

Official Receiver, the bankrupt stated that he had carried on business as a builder for many years past, and this was his third failure. In 1873 he was insolvent, with liabilities £20,000, and no dividend was paid, and in 1887 he again failed, and paid a composition of 5s. in the pound. For some time before 1892 he was building under contracts, but then started operations on his own account. He was then solvent, but had no surplus of assets. He commenced building, shops and offices in Eldon Street, Finsbury, which he estimated would cost £12,000. He obtained an advance of £10,000 on the buildings which he completed at a total cost of about £13,000. He was solely dependent upon advances to carry out his operations. Having erected the premises, however, he was unable to let them fully. Their total letting value was about £3,700, and at the present time they were let to the amount of £1,600 only. In July, 1892, he started putting up warehouses, &c., in Mitre Street, Aldgate, which, however, having erected, he was unable to let entirely. His failure was also partly due to the cost of obtaining money to carry out his building operations and to pressure by creditors. The examination was eventually concluded.

RUMBOLL, FREDERICK WILLIAM, builders' merchant, 9, Morley Square, Bishopston, Bristol, formerly trading as the Montpelier Builders' Depôt, Montpelier Station, Bristol.—The public examination of this bankrupt took place at the Bristol Bankruptcy Court on Friday last, before the Registrar. Replying to questions put by the Assistant Official Receiver, the debtor stated that the reason he did not file his petition before was because he did not know what to do. He admitted that he assigned to his largest creditor certain goods three or four years ago. The examination was ordered to be adjourned.

STOREY, GEORGE, builder, North Runcton.—The public examination of this debtor took place at the last sitting of the Lynn Bankruptcy Court, before the Registrar. The statement of affairs filed by the debtor showed liabilities expected to rank against the estate for dividend amounting to £491 14s. 5d., and the assets were estimated to produce £73 0s. 2d. The debtor, in answer to questions, stated that he commenced business in 1883, with a capital of £30 which he had saved. He took a contract for £600 to do some work to North Runcton Church, but knowing nothing of specifications he lost £85 over it. He was in a worse position at the time he gave the bill of sale than he was when he filed his petition. He had been in the habit of borrowing money from money-lenders and had thereby sunk deeper into the mire. The Court refused to allow the debtor to pass his examination.
